usage: Koreans say 우리 ('our'), not 제 ('my'), for family members
댁 is the honorific word for an elder's home, replacing 집
닮다 takes 을/를; 외삼촌을 닮았어요 = I take after him
오시다 adds 시 because an uncle outranks you
examples: 외삼촌이 두 분 계세요.
I have two maternal uncles.
분 counts people respectfully and 계세요 is the honorific 'there are'
명절에 외삼촌 댁에 가요.
On the holidays I go to my maternal uncle's house.
명절 = traditional holiday; the particle 에 marks both time and destination
외삼촌이 대학 등록금을 보태 주셨어요.
My maternal uncle chipped in for my college tuition.
보태 주시다 = kindly help pay; 주시다 shows the favor came from an elder
nuance: 외삼촌 is specifically your mother's brother. It is built from 한자 外 (oe, 'outside/maternal') + 삼촌 三寸 ('three degrees of kinship'), so it literally frames the mother's side as the 'outside' line — a window into how traditional Korean families centered on the father. The sharp contrast to learn is the pair 삼촌 vs 외삼촌: bare 삼촌 defaults to your FATHER's (unmarried) brother, while the 외 prefix swings it to the maternal side, and that same 외 reappears in 외할머니, 외할아버지, 외사촌. English collapses all of this into one word 'uncle,' which is the core pitfall — you cannot translate 'my uncle' into Korean without first deciding whose side and, often, married or not. Register is neutral and used constantly in everyday family talk; just remember to pair it with honorific verbs (계시다, 오시다, 주시다) and with 우리 rather than 제, since Koreans treat relatives as collectively 'ours.'

mistakes: Dropping 외 and saying 삼촌 for your mom's brother — bare 삼촌 points to your father's side, so you have named the wrong uncle entirely.
Translating 'my uncle' as 제 외삼촌 — for family Koreans almost always say 우리 외삼촌, and 제 sounds oddly detached.
Confusing 외삼촌 (mom's brother) with 외숙모, who is his WIFE; the man himself is never 외숙모.

usage: said only by the husband's parents about their son's wife
들어오다 ('come in') is the set image of marrying into a household
보다 here means 'acquire (in-law)', not 'see'; said when a son marries
맏 ('eldest') marks the daughter-in-law with the heaviest family duties
examples: 우리 며느리예요.
This is my daughter-in-law.
spoken by the in-laws when introducing her; 예요 follows a vowel
며느리가 김치를 직접 담가요.
My daughter-in-law makes kimchi from scratch herself.
직접 = in person/by oneself; 담그다 is the verb for making fermented food
올해 드디어 며느리를 봤어요.
This year we finally gained a daughter-in-law.
보다 = acquire an in-law; 드디어 ('finally') hints the son married at last
nuance: 며느리 is the word a husband's parents use for their son's wife; it is a pure-Korean (고유어) kinship term, not Sino-Korean. The crucial thing English speakers miss is that it is defined from ONE direction only — the in-laws' side — so a woman never calls herself 며느리 when chatting with her own friends; she would say 결혼했어요 or 시댁(her husband's family). Contrast it sharply with its mirror term 사위 (the daughter's husband): 며느리 = son's wife, 사위 = daughter's husband, and mixing them up is the classic beginner slip. Note the idiom 며느리를 보다, where 보다 does NOT mean 'see' but 'gain an in-law' — the natural way to announce that a son has married. Culturally the word carries weight: the 며느리, especially the 맏며느리 (eldest son's wife), traditionally shoulders cooking and ancestral-rite duties, so the term often appears in talk about holidays and family obligation. Register is ordinary spoken Korean.

usage: said only by the wife's parents about their daughter's husband
보다 = acquire an in-law, not 'see'; said when a daughter marries
듬직하다 ('reliable, solid') is a stock compliment for a 사위
an idiom: a 사위 is forever treated like an honored guest
examples: 우리 사위예요.
This is my son-in-law.
spoken by the wife's parents introducing him; 예요 after a vowel
사위가 장인어른을 모시고 왔어요.
My son-in-law brought my father-in-law along (respectfully).
모시고 오다 = escort an elder; 장인어른 = wife's father
지난달에 둘째 사위를 봤어요.
Last month we gained our second son-in-law.
둘째 = the second (daughter's husband); 보다 = acquire an in-law
nuance: 사위 is the word a wife's parents use for their daughter's husband — the exact male mirror of 며느리. It is a native Korean term, and like 며느리 it is anchored to one viewpoint (the in-laws'), so a man does not introduce himself as 사위 in casual conversation; from his side those people are his 처가 (wife's family). The dividing line to drill is 사위 vs 며느리: 사위 = daughter's husband, 며느리 = son's wife. Watch the idiom 사위를 보다, where 보다 means 'gain an in-law,' not 'see' — the natural way to say a daughter has married. Culturally a 사위 is famously pampered: the saying 사위는 백년손님 ('a son-in-law is a hundred-year guest') means the wife's family treats him with lasting hospitality, the opposite of the duty-laden image attached to a 며느리. The English pitfall is that 'son-in-law' is symmetrical in English, but Korean forces you to know which spouse's parents are speaking before you can pick 사위 or 며느리.

usage: 통하다 = go via; the go-to phrase for how introductions or news travel
소개 = introduction; 으로 marks the means by which something happened
가깝다 = close; narrows 지인 to someone you actually know well
업계 = the trade/field; common in work and networking talk
examples: 지인이 좀 있어요.
I have a few acquaintances (here).
좀 softens the statement; 있다 = have/exist
지인의 소개로 지금 회사에 들어왔어요.
I joined my current company through an acquaintance's introduction.
소개로 = by introduction; 들어오다 = enter/join (a company)
그건 그냥 지인한테 들은 얘기예요.
That's just something I heard from an acquaintance.
한테 = from (a person); marks 지인 as the distant, unnamed source
nuance: 지인 means an acquaintance — someone you know but who is not a close 친구. It is Sino-Korean, 한자 知人, literally 知 ('know') + 人 ('person'), i.e. 'a known person,' and that bookish origin is why it sounds a notch more formal than everyday speech. The key contrast is 지인 vs 친구: a 친구 implies warmth, shared time, and usually rough age-equality, whereas 지인 deliberately keeps a polite, neutral distance and says nothing about closeness or age — perfect for a colleague-of-a-colleague or a business contact. You will see it most in writing, news, and careful polite speech, especially in the fixed phrases 지인을 통해 and 지인의 소개로 (how Koreans describe getting jobs, apartments, or tips through personal networks). Two pitfalls for English speakers: do not stretch 'acquaintance' to mean a real friend (use 친구 for that), and resist treating 지인 as casual chit-chat vocabulary — it is the slightly elevated, written-leaning choice, where 아는 사람 ('someone I know') is the plainer spoken equivalent.
